newsitem.title: USA: Foster Wheeler to appeal lawsuit dismissal.
newsitem.headline: Foster Wheeler to appeal lawsuit dismissal.

text.p: Foster Wheeler Corp. said Friday it will appeal the dismissal of its lawsuit against Illinois officials involving a bond-financed incinerator the company built in Robbins, Ill.
The company charged an Illinois law abolishing state subsidies for incinerators violated contract terms, threatened the viability of the roughly $400 million project and could bankrupt the host city.

Tom O'Brien, Foster Wheeler's chief counsel, said an appeal would be filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals, while the company also considered filing another lawsuit in state court and seeks administrative relief from state agencies.
"We're committed to the lawsuit," he said, adding that the ruling by U.S. District Court Judge James Zagel was made strictly on procedural grounds.
In dismissing the lawsuit, Zagel cited the 11th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which precludes lawsuits against states dealing with public funds.

In his 13-page ruling, Zagel said the defendants -- Illinois Gov. Jim Edgar and the members of the Illinois Commerce Commission -- were immune under the amendment. Zagel added that while the claims in the lawsuit "may very well have merit," they should be litigated in state court and not federal court.

The lawsuit, filed by Foster Wheeler, its Illinois subsidiaries and the village of Robbins, charged the state's repeal of a 1987 subsidy for incinerators in March caused the unconstitutional impairment of contract and also violated various U.S. Constitutional provisions, including equal protection and due process.

Clinton, N.J.-based Foster Wheeler filed suit shortly after Edgar in March signed into law a repeal of the Retail Rate Act, which helped incinerators sell electricity to utilities at a higher rate. Edgar's office did not immediately comment on Zagel's ruling.
Robbins' attorney Mark Sterk called the ruling "disastrous" for the impoverished Chicago suburb.
"The success and continued viability of the project really determines if the village will exist," Sterk said, adding the suburb was nearly bankrupt before the incinerator was built.
